title: Solomon's Prayer at the Dedication
summary: Solomon blesses the assembly and praises God for keeping his promise to David. Then, kneeling on a bronze platform before all Israel, he prays a long dedication prayer: he asks God to keep his promise to David's line, confesses that heaven itself cannot contain God, and pleads that whenever his people, or even a foreigner, pray toward this house in sin, defeat, drought, plague, war, or exile, God will hear from heaven and forgive. He closes by calling on God to arise and enter his resting place.
story: The glory cloud has just filled the house (5:13-14). Solomon responds with words. His speech and prayer interpret what the temple means: not a home that confines God, but a place toward which Israel can turn in every kind of trouble and be heard. This prayer functions almost as a charter for the rest of 2 Chronicles. Again and again later kings will face defeat, drought, invasion, and exile, and the question will be whether they turn and pray as Solomon asked. God's reply comes in chapter 7.
historical:
The prayer is found nearly word for word in 1 Kings 8:12-53. The Chronicler adds verse 13, describing the bronze platform (about seven and a half feet square and four and a half feet high, or roughly 2.3 by 2.3 by 1.4 meters) on which Solomon stood and knelt. He also changes the ending. Kings closes with an appeal to God's choice of Israel at the exodus through Moses (1 Kings 8:50-53); Chronicles closes with lines from Psalm 132:8-10, a psalm about David's vow to find a resting place for the ark. The change puts the emphasis on David, the ark, and the temple, the Chronicler's central themes.

For the Chronicler's readers, the petition about exile in verses 36 to 39 was not hypothetical. Their parents and grandparents had been carried captive to Babylon, and many had prayed toward a ruined Jerusalem. Later Jewish practice of praying toward Jerusalem, reflected in Daniel 6:10, grows from this prayer.
cultural:
Solomon prays standing, then kneeling, with hands spread out toward heaven (verses 12-13), the common posture of prayer in the ancient world, palms open and lifted. That a king should kneel publicly before God was itself a statement: Israel's king was not divine and was himself a petitioner.

The language of God's "Name" dwelling in the temple (verses 5-10, 20, 33-34, 38) comes from Deuteronomy, which speaks of the place the LORD will choose to put his Name (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11). In the ancient world a name stood for a person's reputation, authority, and presence. To say that God's Name is in the temple is to say that he is truly present and can be called on there, while he himself dwells in heaven. The oath in verse 22 reflects an ancient legal practice: where evidence was lacking, a person could swear before the altar, and God was trusted to judge the truth.
literary: The chapter has three parts: a short declaration (verses 1-2), a speech of blessing to the people (3-11), and the long prayer (12-42). The prayer itself has a clear shape. After praise and a request that God keep his promise to David (14-17), Solomon asks the chapter's great question, “will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth?” (verse 18). Then comes a series of seven specific petitions (22-39), each beginning with a situation ("When...") and ending with a request that God hear from heaven: a disputed oath, defeat in battle, drought, famine and plague, the foreigner, war, and captivity. The refrain “hear from heaven” and the verbs "forgive" and "return" run through the whole. The closing verses (40-42) turn to poetry drawn from Psalm 132.

outline.t: Solomon blesses the assembly and praises God's faithfulness
Solomon kneels and prays for the promise to David
Can God dwell on earth? A plea to hear from heaven
Petitions for justice, defeat, drought, and plague
The foreigner who prays toward this house
Petitions for war and for exile
Arise, O LORD, to your resting place

doctrines.note: The whole chapter is a lesson in prayer: its posture (kneeling, hands open), its grounds (God's promise and loving devotion), and its range (every kind of trouble, public and private). Solomon asks that God hear not only the king's prayer but the prayer of every person who knows “his own afflictions” (verse 29).

Most of the petitions assume that trouble has come because of sin, and they ask that when the people turn back, confess, and pray, God will forgive. The words Solomon gives the exiles, “We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly” (verse 37), became a model confession for later generations.

“Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You” (verse 18). Solomon builds a house for God while confessing that God cannot be housed. The God of Israel is both truly present with his people and infinitely beyond them.

Solomon prays for the foreigner who comes because of God's great name, asking God to answer him so that “all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You” (verse 33). The temple was meant to draw the nations, not only to serve Israel.

words.note: Shama, to hear, listen, or obey. It appears twelve times in the prayer, which is essentially an extended plea that God would hear. In Hebrew, hearing often implies acting on what is heard: when God hears, he responds.

Salach, to forgive or pardon. In the Old Testament this verb has only God as its subject; people are never said to salach one another. Solomon's repeated request that God forgive (verses 21, 25, 27, 30, 39) rests on a mercy only God can give.

Shuv, to turn or return, and in this sense to repent. It is the Old Testament's main word for repentance: turning around, coming back to God. In verses 24, 26, 37, and 38 the people's turning back is the condition for God's forgiveness and restoration.

Mashiach, anointed one, from which the word Messiah comes. In verse 42 it refers to Solomon, the anointed king of David's line. Later Jewish hope used the same word for the coming king of David's line, and the Greek equivalent is Christos, Christ.

christ: Solomon's question, “will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth?” (verse 18), is answered in the New Testament by the incarnation: in Jesus, God did dwell with human beings on earth. Jesus also redirected the promise of this chapter. When he cleared the temple courts he quoted Isaiah's words that God's house would be called a house of prayer for all the nations (Mark 11:17), fulfilling Solomon's hope for the foreigner in verses 32-33. He told the Samaritan woman that the time was coming when worship would no longer be tied to a mountain or to Jerusalem (John 4:21-24). And the petition that closes the prayer, “do not reject Your anointed one”, looks toward the anointed son of David whom God would not reject. The New Testament presents Jesus as that Messiah, the one through whom prayer is heard and sin forgiven, and it calls him the place where God and people meet. This does not mean Solomon foresaw Jesus in detail; it means his prayer asked for things that God finally gave in Christ.

hard.q: Did Israel believe God actually lived in the temple?
hard.a:
Solomon says both that he has built God “an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever” (verse 2) and that heaven itself cannot contain God (verse 18). The prayer then asks God again and again to hear “from heaven, Your dwelling place”. Readers sometimes see a contradiction, or a development from an older belief that God lived in the temple to a later belief that he lived in heaven.

Most interpreters see the tension as deliberate and theological. The Old Testament holds together God's transcendence (he is above and beyond all creation) and his immanence (he is truly present in particular places and ways). The temple was a real meeting place where God's Name, his reputation and personal presence, dwelt and where his glory could be seen, but it was never his container. Some scholars do trace a development in Israel's thought, especially associated with Deuteronomy's language of the Name; others argue that both ideas were present from the beginning. Either way, the prayer itself insists on both: God is here, and God is not confined here. The prophets would later warn that treating the temple as a guarantee of God's presence, regardless of the people's faithfulness, was a deadly error (Jeremiah 7).

questions: Solomon's prayer covers courtroom disputes, drought, plague, war, and exile. What does it say about God that no situation falls outside what he is willing to hear?

Most of the petitions assume trouble has come through sin, and ask for forgiveness when people turn back. How do you tell the difference between trouble that calls for repentance and trouble that doesn't?
Solomon prayed for foreigners who would come to know Israel's God. Who are the outsiders you pray for?
